items.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005
items.q: There was nothing like that, like the Dorsey brothers? Oh no.

ctx.x: Was there sibling rivalry between you guys?
No, no, no. Oh never, never. We respected each other. I never picked on my brothers because they couldn’t play what I play, no. There was nothing like that, like the Dorsey brothers? Oh no.
Oh yeah. No fist fights over the music. That’s great.

items.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005
items.q: That’s why Jimmy Dorsey wasn’t too well known for his jazz clarinet playing, because he was different, he was entirely different.

ctx.x: Well you got to be known as someone who could handle just about any kind of music that was put in front of you. You had that reputation.

Oh God yeah that’s a good question. You did call for a date and it didn’t matter what the date was. I didn’t get called so much for Dixieland or jazz, you know. I was not really known as a jazz player. I was an improviser. But you know the guy’s jealous — oh he doesn’t play like so-and-so, unless you sounded like Benny or Shaw you were no good. If you had your own style, you know. That’s why Jimmy Dorsey wasn’t too well known for his jazz clarinet playing, because he was different, he was entirely different.

items.title: Spiegle Willcox and Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Norwich, New York, November 14, 1995
items.q: Jimmy, and I knew him pretty well

ctx.x: Yeah. And he influenced people after him also.
I have to mention the famous saxophonist that I admired to this day, Jimmy Dorsey.

items.title: Spiegle Willcox and Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Norwich, New York, November 14, 1995
items.q: And then in the Whiteman band, Paul Whiteman took over Jimmy Dorsey and Tommy Dorsey... from the Goldkette band.

ctx.x: Oh, yeah, I’m glad you said big band. You know I want to tell you something, Monk and Spiegle. The Whiteman band was never really appreciated. We did it all. We went from five saxes to seven saxes to nine saxes. We had great jazz players, the Teagarden brothers, Frankie Trumbauer, great trumpet, and great arrangements. But ‘til this day I respect Glenn Miller, I respect Benny Goodman, but nobody ever had the exposure on television and radio and television that Paul Whiteman did. We had all kinds of hours, the…
Yeah you guys share a lot of the same band mates. I know in your pictures you showed me in your home, some of the same fellows you just mentioned and the Dorsey brothers.

See they all went, the Goldkette band broke up in 1927 around Labor Day, and history shows you that Joe and Eddie Lang always performed together you know, Eddie Lang, and I was very close. And then in the Whiteman band, Paul Whiteman took over Jimmy Dorsey and Tommy Dorsey and Bill Rank, and Steve Brown the bass player and let’s see there was other guys that went in that band, from the Goldkette band. But as you know the history was that I stopped playing, I mean really professional, in 1927. I went home in the…
